strengths: Novel and mathematically clean adaptation of the Mean Flow consistency formalism (Geng et al., 2025a) to deterministic Hamiltonian dynamics. The forward-consistency derivation in Equations (6)-(9) is correct, and the trajectory-free loss in Equation (10) is a genuinely new training objective that requires only instantaneous (x, p, v, f) tuples rather than time-ordered trajectory data.

The core practical claim—that large-timestep flow maps can be trained directly on widely-available decorrelated MLFF datasets (SPICE, QCML, OMol25) without teacher MLFF distillation or trajectory generation—is a meaningful and useful advance over trajectory-based approaches such as FlashMD and TrajCast.

Broad and reasonably convincing empirical validation: single-particle systems (Barbanis, spring pendulum), gravitational N-body, five MD17 molecules, paracetamol, and alanine dipeptide. Results show ~4x fewer integration steps in the N-body task and stable NVT simulations up to 9-12 fs versus a 0.5 fs MLFF+VV baseline, with wall-clock gains (378.5 ns/day vs 31.7 for their own MLFF, Table 7).

The paper honestly reports limitations, including the degradation of instantaneous force accuracy relative to a dedicated MLFF (Table 8), the systematic failure at Δt≈10 fs for alanine dipeptide (Table 15, PMF error 29.676), and the fact that inference filters do not by themselves enable larger timesteps (Figure 21).

Reproducibility is strong: detailed appendices specify architectures, conditioning, timestep-sampling distributions, momentum sampling, filters, thermostats, training hyperparameters, and compute infrastructure; the coupled energy/angular-momentum projection is derived in closed form (Appendix B.3).

The coupled energy+angular-momentum conservation filter is a nice technical contribution that improves on decoupled/sequential correction schemes, and the ablation showing that filters restore per-element equipartition (Table 14) is informative.
weaknesses: The central motivation is that HFMs outperform trajectory-based large-timestep models (FlashMD, TrajCast, Bigi et al.), yet no head-to-head empirical comparison with any of these methods is provided. The only baseline is Velocity Verlet with an MLFF (or the ground-truth potential for the classical/N-body systems). Without comparing accuracy at matched Δt, data efficiency, or cost against the very methods the paper positions itself against, the claimed advantage remains asserted rather than demonstrated.

The inference-time filters (random rotation, drift removal, coupled E&L conservation) plus an auxiliary MLFF or extra energy head carry substantial weight in the reported stability and thermodynamic accuracy. The paper argues (Figure 21) that filters do not enable larger timesteps on their own, but the reliance on a non-equivariant, non-conservative architecture that must be corrected post-hoc reduces the elegance of the contribution and complicates the fairness of the wall-clock comparison (the extra potential-energy evaluation is folded into the reported 2.1 ms/step).

The systematic instability at Δt≈10 fs for alanine dipeptide is reported but not explained. The claim that it 'does not consistently correlate with one-step prediction error' is unsatisfying, and it undermines the generality of the large-timestep claim for the most chemically relevant system studied.

Instantaneous force MAE is consistently worse than a dedicated MLFF (Table 8), and the tradeoff is controlled only by the heuristic q_{Δt=0}=0.75. The sufficiency argument (Appendix C) is brief and essentially cites the Mean Flow proof rather than providing a rigorous treatment for the Hamiltonian setting, including the effect of stop-gradient and the finite-Δt regularization.

Some experimental choices make the comparisons harder to interpret: in the classical/N-body cases the HFM uses the ground-truth potential inside its conservation filter while VV also uses the ground-truth potential, so the comparison isolates the integrator but not the overall system; in MD the HFM uses its own trained MLFF as the energy-correction potential, adding coupling that is not ablated in the main results.

strengths: Correct and clearly presented core contribution: the paper derives a trajectory-free consistency objective (Eqs. 7–10, Algorithm 1) by adapting the Mean Flow identity to deterministic Hamiltonian phase-space dynamics. The derivation (product rule + fundamental theorem of calculus + chain rule along the flow) is mathematically sound, and the Δt=0 limit correctly reduces to standard force matching (Eq. 11).

The central practical idea is genuinely useful: large-timestep maps can be trained on independent snapshots with instantaneous force labels only, avoiding the expensive trajectory generation and teacher-MLFF bias that afflict trajectory-based methods (FlashMD, TrajCast). This is directly relevant for ab-initio/MLFF datasets that contain decorrelated geometries.

A real and well-demonstrated insight: because the model learns the *dynamics* (the flow) rather than the equilibrium distribution, it recovers correct NVT statistics even from biased/sparse training data (Figure 7, 256-sample paracetamol), whereas the distribution-matching ScoreMD reproduces the biased training distribution. This property is non-trivial and nicely validated against a generative baseline.

Broad and well-structured empirical study spanning classical mechanics (Barbanis, spring pendulum, gravitational 100-body) and MD (four MD17 molecules, paracetamol, alanine dipeptide), including a 1 ms alanine-dipeptide simulation at Δt=12 fs that captures metastable transitions (Figure 8).

Thorough ablations: τ-sampling distributions (Appendix G.6), effect of inference filters on thermodynamics and spectra (G.10), thermostat sensitivity (G.4), semi-group/consistency analysis (G.8), training-horizon trade-offs (G.7), and stability tables (G.5). These strengthen confidence in the reported behavior.

The coupled energy- and angular-momentum-conservation filter (Appendix B.3) is a clean, closed-form technical contribution that avoids interference between the two constraints, and the paper honestly shows filters do not artificially stabilize Velocity Verlet (G.10).
The limitations section and appendices are candid about the non-symplectic nature of the learned map, the role of filters, and the difficulty of training in chaotic/large-Δt regimes.
weaknesses: No direct empirical comparison to the most relevant trajectory-based large-timestep methods that the paper positions itself against (FlashMD, Bigi et al. 2025a; TrajCast, Thiemann et al. 2025). The only integration baseline is MLFF + Velocity Verlet at 0.5 fs, a weak comparator. Consequently, the central positioning claim—that trajectory-free training is a viable *alternative* at comparable quality—is not substantiated empirically.

Overclaiming of physical structure. The method learns a generic (non-equivariant, non-symplectic) neural flow-map approximation; Hamiltonian/symplectic structure, energy conservation, and equivariance are only approximately preserved and are largely restored by post-hoc inference filters plus an auxiliary potential/energy head. The name 'Hamiltonian Flow Map' and the framing overstate the physical consistency actually enforced by the model.

Systematic and unexplained instability at intermediate timesteps: for alanine dipeptide, PMF error jumps to 29.7 and MJS to 0.54 at Δt≈10 fs (Table 15), then recovers at 11–13 fs. This non-monotonic failure is attributed vaguely to 'inherent instability' and directly undercuts the robustness narrative and the claim of stable large-timestep rollouts.

The accuracy/speed trade-off is real and understated in the abstract: at large Δt the structural error grows substantially (e.g., ethanol 0.073→0.115 from 0.5 to 9 fs), so the practical sweet spot is modest (≈3–5 fs). Reported speedups (e.g., 12× for aspirin) come with meaningful accuracy degradation that is not quantified in the headline claims.

Training cost and reproducibility concerns. Reported training times are large (up to 3d12h–4d22h for alanine dipeptide; 1d11h for small molecules, versus 16h for the MLFF baseline), making the 'comparable training cost' claim generous; no code release is mentioned, and reproducing the results would require substantial compute.

Moderate methodological novelty: the mathematical machinery is transplanted from Mean Flow (Geng et al. 2025a) and the sufficiency argument (Appendix C) is inherited rather than newly established. The contribution is primarily the adaptation and its application to MD.

The classical-mechanics training regime (positions uniformly sampled at fixed total energy with exact analytic forces) is idealized and may not reflect the biased/correlated distributions encountered in practice; all evaluated molecular systems are small (≤~22 atoms), limiting evidence for scalability.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated trajectory-free training objective: the authors adapt the Mean Flow consistency formalism to deterministic Hamiltonian dynamics using a forward (start-time) consistency condition (Eqs. 6-9), which is derived cleanly and correctly via the product rule, the fundamental theorem of calculus, and the chain rule.

Removes the need for expensive trajectory generation or teacher MLFF distillation by training directly on standard decorrelated ab-initio MLFF datasets (positions + force labels, with momenta sampled from Maxwell-Boltzmann), which is a practically meaningful advance over trajectory-based large-timestep methods.

Broad and well-structured empirical validation: two analytic single-particle systems (Barbanis, spring pendulum), a 100-body gravitational system, four MD17 molecules, paracetamol, and alanine dipeptide. The N-body result (4x fewer steps than Velocity Verlet to reach equal accuracy) and the 1 ms alanine dipeptide rollout are convincing.

Practical wall-clock gains are demonstrated (Table 7): HFM-9fs reaches ~378 ns/day vs ~31.7 ns/day for the MLFF baseline and ~148.9 ns/day for lightweight SchNet, even accounting for the auxiliary energy MLFF call.

Strong data-efficiency result (Fig. 7): an HFM trained on only 256 decorrelated samples recovers the reference conformational distribution and vibrational spectrum, whereas ScoreMD reproduces the biased training distribution.

Good control experiments and ablation discipline: Appendix G.10 shows the inference filters do not rescue Velocity Verlet (indeed they cause earlier divergence), supporting the claim that large-timestep stability comes from the learned map rather than post-hoc projection. The coupled energy+angular-momentum conservation filter is a clean, closed-form, novel contribution.
Reproducibility is well supported: detailed architecture tables, hyperparameters, optimizer settings, software licenses, and public datasets (MD17, alanine dipeptide) are provided.
Limitations are discussed honestly (approximate preservation of symplecticity/energy/equivariance, instability near the training horizon, thermostat-dependent artifacts, chaotic-regime difficulty).
weaknesses: The most directly comparable baselines — trajectory-based large-timestep models such as FlashMD (Bigi et al., 2025a) and TrajCast (Thiemann et al., 2025) — are not compared against experimentally. Since the paper's central value proposition is that trajectory-free training is competitive, a head-to-head accuracy/speed comparison against these methods is needed to establish the claim; the only learned large-timestep comparison (ScoreMD) targets equilibrium sampling rather than deterministic propagation.

The method relies on several inference-time filters, including an auxiliary MLFF (or extra prediction head) for energy evaluation. This adds architectural complexity and per-step cost, and partially undercuts the clean 'trajectory-free, end-to-end' framing, even though the authors argue (persuasively) that the filters are not doing the heavy lifting.
Force-field accuracy is worse than a dedicated MLFF (Table 8: e.g., salicylic acid 6.0 vs 2.2 meV/Å), which weakens the 'single model that is simultaneously a force field and an integrator' claim.

Accuracy degrades noticeably with timestep (Table 1, e.g., ethanol 0.076 -> 0.115 from 1 fs to 9 fs), and an unexplained instability appears near ~10 fs for alanine dipeptide that does not correlate with one-step error (Appendix G.11), suggesting the learned map's interaction with the simulation setup is not fully understood.

Some negative/awkward results are only partially addressed: the deterministic Nosé-Hoover thermostat produces large artifacts (Table 10), which limits the generality of the NVT results to stochastic thermostats.

Presentation issues: the reference list contains systematically wrong bracket years (e.g., Geng et al. labeled 2023 for 2025 papers, DDPM labeled 2023, Adam labeled 2023), plus typos ('paracetmol', 'Durmeric' vs 'Durumeric'). These should be corrected but do not affect the scientific content.

strengths: Introduces a trajectory-free training objective for Hamiltonian flow maps based on a mean-flow consistency condition, enabling training from single-time phase-space samples without trajectory generation or teacher models.

Provides a theoretical justification (Appendix C) showing the consistency condition is sufficient for learning the true flow map, and derives an efficient training algorithm using Jacobian-vector products and stop-gradient.

Demonstrates large-timestep stability across diverse systems: classical potentials, a 100-body gravitational system, MD17/MD22 molecules, alanine dipeptide, and coarse-grained proteins, often with 10-20x speedups over MLFF baselines.

Shows strong data efficiency and robustness to biased/sparse training distributions (e.g., 256 paracetamol samples recover correct free energy surfaces), and compares favorably to trajectory-matching objectives under fixed force-evaluation budgets.

Proposes a coupled energy/angular momentum conservation filter and shows it does not artificially stabilize incorrect Velocity Verlet steps, supporting that large-timestep stability stems from the learned map.
Extensive appendices with implementation details, hyperparameters, additional ablations, and an honest limitations discussion.
weaknesses: Lacks direct comparison to prior learned large-timestep methods (e.g., FlashMD, TrajCast) in the main experiments; only an indirect comparison to a trajectory-matching objective appears in the appendix, making it difficult to assess whether HFM outperforms existing large-timestep models.

Training cost claims are not clearly supported: the abstract says 'comparable training and inference cost', but Appendix F shows HFM training times up to 2-4x longer than the MLFF baseline (e.g., 1d11h vs 16h for small molecules; 22h vs 13h for paracetamol) due to many more epochs. The '30% overhead' statement likely refers to per-step compute, but this is ambiguous.

Relies on multiple inference filters (random rotation, drift removal, coupled energy/angular momentum conservation) and an additional potential energy evaluation (via extra head or MLFF), adding complexity and cost; without filters, thermodynamic drift is observed. The method is not purely trajectory-free at inference if an MLFF is needed for the energy filter.

The learned map is not symplectic or exactly equivariant; physical constraints are enforced post hoc. Long-term stability and accuracy degrade at larger timesteps (e.g., ethanol 9 fs h(r) MAE 0.115 vs MLFF 0.073; alanine dipeptide shows large PMF errors at 10-11 fs), and some simulations collapse, indicating robustness limits.
Missing code/weights URL in the manuscript (likely due to anonymization) and incomplete details on how the energy head is trained for the conservation filter may hinder reproducibility.

Restricts to separable Hamiltonians and requires sampling momenta from Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions, limiting applicability to systems with non-separable Hamiltonians or where momentum distribution is unknown.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely novel and well motivated: adapting the Mean Flow self-distillation consistency identity (Geng et al., 2025a) to *deterministic* Hamiltonian dynamics yields an integral-free training objective that learns a mean displacement field from single-time phase-space samples plus instantaneous force labels. This removes the need for reference trajectories, which are prohibitively expensive at ab-initio accuracy, and is a real conceptual advance over trajectory-regression approaches (Bigi et al., 2025a; Thiemann et al., 2026).

The technical core is correct: I verified the consistency derivation (Eqs. 6-9) and the induced regression target (Eq. 10). Differentiating Delta-t * u-bar = integral(v,f) and applying Leibniz gives u-bar - Delta-t du-bar/dt = (v_t, f_t), which is exactly Eq. 8, and the chain rule in Eq. 9 is correct. The resulting loss is a valid self-consistency fixed point that reduces to standard force matching at Delta-t = 0 (Eq. 11), giving a single model that acts as both a force field and a large-step integrator.

The empirical validation is broad and spans an unusually wide range of scales: 1D toys (Barbanis, spring pendulum), a 100-body gravitational system, MD17 small molecules, paracetamol, alanine dipeptide, Ac-Ala3-NHMe, and coarse-grained Chignolin/BBA. Stable rollouts are demonstrated at 9-45 fs where Velocity Verlet is unstable, and the model recovers structural (h(r), Ramachandran), temporal (vibrational spectra, transition rates), and Lyapunov-time statistics.

Several concrete and reusable contributions beyond the main idea: a closed-form coupled energy-and-angular-momentum conservation filter (App. B.3) that avoids interference between the two constraints, an adaptive/timestep-sampling scheme, and a controlled data-efficiency study (App. G.14) showing HFM beats trajectory-matching at equal force-labeling budgets. The control experiment in App. G.11 (filters do not rescue VV at large steps) is a thoughtful check against the obvious confound.

Reproducibility is strong: code, model weights, and self-contained JAX/PyTorch notebooks are promised; the appendix provides architecture tables, batch sizes, epoch counts, wall-clock times, hardware, and software licenses.

Limitations are discussed honestly (approximate symplecticity/equivariance, reliance on filters and thermostats, difficulty of optimization in chaotic regimes, alanine-dipeptide instability at ~10 fs).
weaknesses: The sufficiency argument (App. C) is not rigorous. It reduces to an 'integration constant' assertion and a citation to Geng et al. (2025a), rather than proving that any solution of the differentiated consistency condition, subject to the Delta-t = 0 boundary condition, equals the true flow map. The necessity direction is fine, but the central theoretical claim of the paper (that matching instantaneous labels is *sufficient*) is not convincingly established.

The headline 'trajectory-free / no-teacher' advantage is partially undercut in practice. The energy-conservation filter requires an additional potential-energy evaluation, supplied either by a separately trained MLFF or an extra head, so the method is not fully self-contained; and the coarse-grained Chignolin/BBA experiments obtain their force labels by distilling ScoreMD, i.e., a teacher. The framing overstates the degree to which teachers and auxiliary models are avoided.

Accuracy degrades substantially at large timesteps. In Table 1, h(r) MAE at 9 fs is 40-66% higher than the 0.5 fs MLFF baseline (e.g., Ethanol 0.073 -> 0.115), and alanine dipeptide becomes unstable around 10 fs (PMF 29.7, MJS 0.538). The paper's own semi-group consistency analysis (App. G.8) shows the model only matches Velocity Verlet consistency up to ~4 fs, which sits awkwardly with the claim that much larger steps are used 'effectively.'

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The abstract/intro claim 'comparable training cost' is hard to square with the appendix (small molecules: HFM up to 1d11h vs MLFF 16h; paracetamol HFM 22h vs MLFF 13h), even if gradient-step counts happen to match. The comparison to ScoreMD in Figure 7 is also somewhat unfair: a diffusion model trained on a biased dataset reproducing that biased distribution is expected behavior, and the paper itself notes reweighting is required, so this does not cleanly demonstrate HFM superiority.

The architectural choice is unusual and somewhat ad hoc: a translation-invariant (not rotation-equivariant) transformer, with equivariance enforced only via data augmentation plus a random-rotation inference filter that 'averages out' non-equivariance. Given that an SO(3)-equivariant model is used for the baseline, it is surprising that the HFM itself is not equivariant, and this likely leaves accuracy on the table while complicating claims of physical fidelity.

The main-text evaluation of the large-timestep capability relies heavily on the 0.5 fs MLFF + VV baseline; direct head-to-head comparisons against existing large-timestep trajectory-based methods (FlashMD, TrajCast) are largely relegated to appendices and a single data-efficiency study, making it harder to situate the practical gains.

The design is sensitive to several tuned hyperparameters (the mixture q(tau), q_{Delta-t=0}=0.75, q_{L=0}, q_{p=0}), and the loss landscape is acknowledged to be delicate; robustness of these choices across systems is only partially demonstrated.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely useful and non-obvious idea: a trajectory-free training objective for large-timestep Hamiltonian flow maps. By adapting the Mean Flow consistency identity (a start-time rather than end-time derivative) to deterministic Hamiltonian phase-space dynamics, the method learns mean velocity/force fields from only instantaneous (x, f) labels, avoiding the expensive teacher-MLFF trajectory generation required by prior long-timestep work (e.g., FlashMD, TrajCast).

The empirical validation is unusually broad and convincing: 1D toy systems (Barbanis, spring pendulum), a 100-body gravitational system, MD17 small molecules, paracetamol NVE/NVT, MD22 Ac-Ala3-NHMe, alanine dipeptide (1 us), and coarse-grained Chignolin/BBA. The paper reports structural observables (h(r) MAE), temporal observables (vibrational spectra), transition probabilities (Chignolin JSD), Lyapunov times, and conservation of energy/angular momentum, giving a multifaceted picture of physical fidelity.

Practical advantages are well supported: comparable training cost (~30% overhead over MLFF training), a single continuous model that supports arbitrary timesteps up to Δt_max and also recovers instantaneous forces at Δt=0, and a clear wall-clock speedup analysis (Table 9) showing 378.5 ns/day vs 31.7 for their MLFF.

The data-efficiency comparison against trajectory-matching (Tables 19-20, Figures 27-28) is a strong and fair argument for the trajectory-free formulation, showing lower PMF/MJS error at equal force-evaluation budgets, particularly in the low-data regime.

Thoughtful treatment of stability: the coupled energy-and-angular-momentum projection filter is a closed-form, non-trivial contribution, and the ablation in Appendix G.11 (Figure 23) directly tests whether filters artificially stabilize invalid trajectories — showing they do not rescue Velocity Verlet — which is exactly the right control experiment.
Reproducibility is strong: code, model weights, and self-contained JAX/PyTorch notebooks are provided; hyperparameters, data splits, architectures, and training times are documented in detail.
Limitations are discussed honestly (approximate structure preservation, need for filters/thermostats, difficulty of optimization at large Δt in chaotic regimes).
weaknesses: Originality is moderate: the core machinery is an adaptation of Mean Flow (Geng et al., 2025a) and self-distillation consistency models (Boffi et al., 2025a). The domain-specific derivation (start-time derivative, separable-Hamiltonian handling, mass-weighted loss) is meaningful but incremental in the ML-methodology sense.

The sufficiency argument in Appendix C is loose. It shows the consistency condition is necessary and argues (by matching integration constants at Δt=0) that it is also sufficient, but does not rigorously rule out spurious minimizers or establish that stop-gradient optimization converges to the true field. The central theoretical claim is therefore only informally justified, even if empirically supported.

The role of the inference filters is not fully disentangled. While G.11 is a good control, the main results (Table 1, Figure 6-9) all use filters, so the reader cannot easily assess how much of the large-timestep stability comes from the learned map versus the projections. The abstract/intro do not foreground this dependence.

There is an unexplained instability near Δt ≈ 10 fs for alanine dipeptide (Table 17 shows PMF error jumping to 29.7 at 10 fs and 10.5 at 11 fs, then recovering at 12 fs). The hydrogen-vibration-period hypothesis is plausible but not verified, and it raises questions about predictability/robustness of the learned map at particular step sizes.

Instantaneous force accuracy is consistently worse than the MLFF baseline (Table 10: e.g., salicylic acid 6.0 vs 2.2 meV/Å). This is acknowledged, but it means HFMs are not a drop-in replacement for force prediction and require the Δt=0 sampling ratio to be tuned.

Some speedup framing is potentially overstated: the Chignolin 20x speedup is measured against a coarse-grained ScoreMD teacher that the model distills, so the comparison is partly circular and the absolute claim depends on the distillation setup.
Training times are very long (up to ~5 GPU-days per model on A100/H100), which somewhat undercuts the 'comparable compute budget' narrative for practitioners, even if per-step inference is cheap.
